lesson.subtitle: Term 4 Week 4, Session 3
lesson.fileName: Session 3 - Expected Results and More Trials.pptx

plan.curriculum: Mathematics 2.0, Probability, Year 6 (VC2M6P02) with Year 5 (VC2M5P02): compare observations with expected results and discuss the effect of increasing the number of trials, including simulations
plan.shape: example-first: the teacher models expected results, then shows real results settling as trials grow, because the pattern needs to be seen before it is explained
plan.criticalFeature: small experiments vary a lot; with many more trials the relative frequency settles close to the expected chance
decisionPoints: the choice check: what 8 heads in 10 tosses tells us
plan.anchor: chance = the outcomes we want out of all the equally likely outcomes
plan.catchUp: Missed Session 2? Show 12 heads in 20 tosses written as 12/20 = 60% before the launch: that is relative frequency.

manipulatives: A coin and a dice for every pair (optional)
studentTools: Printed Worksheet for every student; Extension and Supported Worksheet as needed
routineIcons: Write it, chin it, show me
boardSetup: The week's anchor on the board: chance = the outcomes we want out of all the equally likely outcomes
Optional simulation: a spreadsheet column of =RANDBETWEEN(1,2) filled down 1000 rows, with 1 as heads

resources.label: Worksheet
resources.description: Your turn. Work out expected results, compare them with observed results, fix a mistake and read a simulation.
resources.title: Expected Results and More Trials
resources.subtitle: Expected = chance × trials. More trials, closer results.

example.prompt: A spinner has P(red) = 1/5. How many reds do you expect in 50 spins?

items.prompt: How many times would you expect each outcome?

parts.prompt: A shooter scores 3 of every 4 shots. Goals from 40 shots?
A keeper saves 1/5 of penalties. Saves from 25?

items.prompt: A batter hits 1 in every 3 balls. She expects 12 hits. How many balls does she face?

example.prompt: Expected 20 heads, observed 23. Is that surprising?

items.prompt: Ella rolled a dice 6 times and got no sixes. Find her mistake and fix it.
work: I got none, so the dice is broken.
items.answer: 6 rolls is far too few to judge. Getting no sixes is common in a small experiment. Roll it many more times.

example.prompt: A simulation tossed a coin 10 times: 70% heads. Is the coin unfair?
steps: 10 tosses is a small number of trials.

items.prompt: Kai tossed a coin and got heads 5 times in a row. What about the next toss?
options: heads and tails are still equally likely
items.explain: A coin has no memory: every toss is still 1/2 heads, 1/2 tails.

resources.label: Extension
resources.description: Early finisher option. Planning a spreadsheet simulation, expected results for unequal spinners and judging fairness from data, with worked examples.
resources.title: Extension: Simulations
resources.subtitle: Use lots of trials to test a prediction.

example.prompt: How could a spreadsheet roll a dice 600 times?
steps: Count each number, then compare with 100 each.

items.prompt: Plan a spreadsheet simulation of 1000 coin tosses. Write the formula, how you would count heads, and what result you predict. If you have a device, try it.
items.answer: =RANDBETWEEN(1,2) filled down 1000 rows; count the 1s (for example =COUNTIF(A1:A1000,1)); predict about 500 heads, close to 50%.

items.prompt: P(red) = 5/12. How many reds would you expect in 360 spins?
A bag has 3 red, 4 blue and 1 white counter. How many whites would you expect in 240 picks, with replacement?

example.prompt: A dice gave 168 sixes in 1000 rolls. Fair?
steps: Fair, as far as we can tell.

items.prompt: A coin gave 703 heads in 1000 tosses. Is it fair? Explain with numbers.
items.answer: Probably not: expected about 500, and 703 is far off after so many trials.

items.prompt: A spinner gave 7 reds in 20 spins, but P(red) = 1/4. Is it unfair? Explain.
items.answer: Not necessarily: expected 5, and 7 is close for only 20 spins. More trials are needed.

slides.notes: Session 3 of our probability week: today we compare results with what we expect, and see what more trials do.

Before you start, put boards and markers on every desk. Optional: set up a spreadsheet simulation with =RANDBETWEEN(1,2) filled down 1000 rows. Print the Worksheet for everyone, and a few copies of the Extension and the Supported Worksheet.

slides.title: Missing corner
prompts: A square has corners (2, 1), (6, 1) and (6, 5). Find the fourth corner.

beats: SAY: Let's warm up with coordinates and statistics.
ASK: What is the fourth corner of this square?
25 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: (2, 5)
SCAN boards, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal and move straight on.
Less -> sketch the three corners on the
board grid and trace up from (2, 1). Re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: It's 2, 5: above 2, 1 and level with 6, 5.
Tick it or fix it.
trap: writing (5, 2).
Fix: say the anchor, across first, and they rewrite it.
notes.prep: Review of Week 2 coordinates (the request named the focus). Keep the review under 6 minutes.

slides.title: Move across zero
prompts: (-3, 2) moves 5 right. Where does it land?

beats: ASK: If negative 3, 2 moves 5 right, where does it land?
20 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: (2, 2)
SCAN boards, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal and move straight on.
Less -> jump 5 right from negative 3 on the number line together. Re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: Negative 3 add 5 is 2,
so it lands on 2, 2. Tick it or fix it.
trap: writing (-8, 2).
Fix: ask which way right goes, and they redo it.

beats: ASK: How many families were surveyed?
20 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 16
SCAN boards, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, then on to Fluency.
Less -> count the dots in each column, then add. Re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: 2, 6, 4, 3 and 1 make 16 families. Tick it or fix it.
trap: writing 5, the number of columns.
Fix: touch each dot as you count, and they recount.
notes.prep: Week 3 review: reading a dot plot.

beats: SAY: Now for our seven times table.
Write each answer as fast as you can.
ASK: What is 7 times 7?
8 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 49
SCAN boards.
80%+ -> reveal, then the next one.
Less -> 6 sevens is 42, then one more 7. Re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: It's 49. Tick it or fix it.
trap: writing 42 or 56.
Fix: add one more 7 to 7 times 6, 42, and they rewrite it.
notes.prep: Times tables fluency. Keep the whole block under 5 minutes.

beats: SAY: Here's the next one.
ASK: What is 7 times 11?
8 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 77
SCAN boards.
80%+ -> reveal, then the next one.
Less -> 7 tens, plus one more 7. Re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: It's 77. Tick it or fix it.
trap: writing 71.
Fix: 7 tens is 70, plus one more 7, and they rewrite it.
notes.prep: Brisk: one line of feedback, then the next.

beats: SAY: Now a division. How many sevens make 56?
ASK: What is 56 divided by 7?
8 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 8
SCAN boards.
80%+ -> reveal, then the learning intention.
Less -> count up in sevens to 56. Re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: It's 8. Tick it or fix it.
trap: writing 7 or 9.
Fix: check: 8 sevens is 56, and they rewrite it.
notes.prep: Brisk: one line of feedback, then the next.

slides.learningIntention: We are learning to compare experiment results with what we expect, and see what happens with more trials.
successCriteria: I can work out the expected result for a chance experiment.
I can compare an observed result with the expected result.
I can explain why more trials give results closer to what we expect.

beats: POINT to the learning intention.
SAY: Yesterday our coin results weren't exactly half.
Today we find out why, and what happens with lots more trials.
SAY: Let's read our I can statements together.
Cue: Everyone, together, on three.
SAY: The first one is where we start,
and the second one is our big goal today.
notes.prep: SC1 expected results is reachable for everyone; SC2 comparing observed and expected is the core and the exit evidence; SC3 the effect of more trials is the stretch.

slides.title: What would you expect?
slides.prompt: Toss a coin 100 times. How many heads would you expect?

beats: SHOW a coin.
SAY: If I tossed this coin 100 times, I wouldn't know exactly what would happen.
ASK: How many heads would you expect in 100 tosses?
10 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 50
ASK: Would 47 heads surprise you? What about 80? Tell your partner why.
20 sec. Cue: Partner A first. You have 20 seconds. Go.
EXPECT: 47 is fine; 80 is surprising
SAY: We expect about 50, because heads is one half.
Today we'll see why 47 is normal, and 80 is unusual after many tosses.
trap: saying exactly 50 every time.
Fix: ask what happened with yesterday's coin, and they rethink.
notes.prep: The launch comes after the LI: expected versus observed. Under 4 minutes.

slides.meaning: The result we predict from the chance: chance times the number of trials.

beats: POINT to the word.
SAY: This word is expected. Say it with me: ex-pect-ed.
SAY: The expected result is what the chance predicts.
We find it by taking that fraction of the number of trials.
ASK: Toss a coin 40 times. How many heads would you expect?
10 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 20
trap: expecting 40 heads.
Fix: ask what fraction of tosses should be heads, and they redo it.
notes.prep: Expected versus observed is today's comparison.

slides.title: Work out the expected result
steps: Take that fraction of the trials: 1/6 of 60.

visual.text: Roll a dice 60 times. How many sixes do you expect?

beats: MODEL finding the chance.
SAY: A six is one face out of six, so the chance is one sixth.
MODEL one sixth of 60.
SAY: So I expect one sixth of the 60 rolls.
60 divided by 6 is 10,
so I expect about 10 sixes. About, because results vary.
ASK: How many sixes would you expect in 120 rolls?
15 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 20
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: One sixth of 120 is 20.
Double the trials, double the expected number.
trap: writing 60 divided by 120.
Fix: say one sixth of the trials, and they redo it.
notes.stretch: How many rolls would give an expected 25 sixes?
notes.help: Draw 6 groups and share the trials equally.

beats: POINT to 10 tosses.
SAY: This graph shows a simulation.
After 10 tosses, 70 percent were heads, far from a half.
POINT along the line.
SAY: As the tosses grow to 100, then 1000,
the line settles closer and closer to 50 percent.
Small experiments jump around; big ones settle.
ASK: What would you expect after 10 000 tosses?
15 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: very close to 50%
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: Very close to 50 percent.
That's why we never judge a coin from 10 tosses.
trap: thinking more trials make it exactly 50%.
Fix: say close, not exact, and they rephrase.
notes.stretch: Why would 1000 tosses rarely give exactly 500 heads?
notes.help: Point to where the line is closest to 50.
notes.prep: The critical feature: more trials, closer to expected. SC3. Optional: run the spreadsheet simulation live.

slides.title: 8 heads in 10 tosses
slides.prompt: What does this tell us? Point to A, B or C

options.misconception: judges the coin from a very small experiment

options.text: The next toss will probably be tails.
options.misconception: thinks the coin remembers and has to even out

beats: SAY: Mia tossed a coin 10 times and got 8 heads.
ASK: What does this result tell us?
15 sec. Cue: Voices off. Point... now. Hold your point.
EXPECT: pointing to B
SCAN the room, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, then cold call one student: Why isn't it C?
Less -> go back to the simulation line: 10 tosses jumped to 70 percent. Re-ask.
REVEAL after pointing is scanned.
SAY: It's B. 10 tosses is too few to judge,
and the coin has no memory, so the next toss is still one half.
trap: pointing to C.
Fix: ask whether the coin knows what came before, and they choose again.
notes.prep: First decision point. A: judging from too few trials. C: the coin has to even out.

slides.title: Expected results
slides.pivot: write the chance, then take that fraction of the trials
slides.followUp: cold call one board: Which fraction did you use?

items.text: Bag: 3 red, 2 blue. 50 picks, replaced. Blue?
items.say: Blue is 2 of 5, so 2/5 of 50 is 20.
One sixth of the rolls is 25, so 6 times 25 is 150 rolls.

say: Write each answer on your board.
trap: using the wrong fraction.
Fix: say the chance first, and they redo it.
notes.stretch: Write a question where the expected answer is 12.
notes.prep: Guided practice: halves, sixths, quarters, fifths, then a reverse question. SC1 and SC2.

slides.title: 20 spins or 2000 spins?

visual.text: Class A spun a spinner 20 times. Class B spun it 2000 times. P(red) = 1/4.

slides.label: Whose relative frequency of red is likely closer to 1/4?

beats: SAY: This one is just for you.
Think about what more trials do.
ASK: Whose relative frequency of red is likely to be closer to one quarter?
Write A or B.
15 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: B
SCAN every board, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, then Your turn.
Less -> point back to the simulation line settling at 50 percent. Re-ask.
REVEAL after boards are scanned.
SAY: It's B. 2000 spins is many more trials,
so the result settles closer to the expected chance. Tick it or fix it.
trap: writing A because 20 is easier to count.
Fix: ask which class has more evidence, and they choose again.
notes.prep: The hinge before independent work. Anyone writing A starts on the Supported Worksheet with the teacher.

slides.title: Your turn
slides.task: Work out expected results and compare them with observed results on your worksheet.

beats: POINT to the steps.
SAY: Read each question carefully, solve it carefully, then check your answers.
SAY: If you finish, the Extension is your early finisher option.
Let's read the steps together. Cue: Everyone, together, on three.
CIRCULATE and ask: What is the chance, and how many trials?
TIME: 20 minutes. Stop everyone once at 10 minutes to share a strategy.
trap: multiplying instead of taking a fraction.
Fix: say 'one sixth of', and they redo it.
notes.stretch: Extension: a spreadsheet simulation, unequal spinners and judging fairness.
notes.help: Supported Worksheet: halves and quarters first, a step frame and hints.
notes.prep: Independent practice: expected results, observed versus expected, a mistake, and a simulation. The sheet is evidence for SC2 and SC3.

slides.title: Show what you know
questions: How many fives would you expect in 300 rolls of a dice?

beats: SAY: Here's the last one. Work it out on your own board.
ASK: How many fives would you expect in 300 rolls of a dice?
25 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: 50
RECORD who multiplies or uses the wrong fraction.
They start tomorrow's check with the teacher.
trap: writing 1800.
Fix: none now. Record the name for tomorrow.
notes.prep: Exit evidence for SC1 and SC2: a new number of trials.

slides.reflectionPrompt: Tell your partner what happens to results with more trials.

notes.answer: open - listen for they get closer to what we expect
beats: SAY: Let's read our I can statements together.
Cue: Everyone, together, on three.
ASK: How sure are you that you can compare results with what you expect?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: thumbs up, sideways or down
RECORD each thumb down beside the exit board.
A thumb up with 1800 on the board matters most.
ASK: What happens to results when you do more trials?
20 sec. Cue: Partner A first. You have 20 seconds. Go.
EXPECT: they get closer to what we expect
notes.prep: Read the self-assessment beside the exit evidence. Tomorrow: fair and unfair games.
